title: AI in the Classroom: New Report Highlights What Parents Want
gist: IFS blog summary of its new YouGov-based report on AI in K-12 schools: about 4 in 10 students attend schools allowing or requiring AI, yet 56% of parents want it fully blocked and most expect more harm than benefit. Support for AI pauses like those in New York City and Los Angeles is bipartisan, and 6 in 10 parents feel AI makes their child's future look bleak or frightening.

themes.theme: Ed-tech backlash sets the stage for AI

insights.claim: Parental backlash against social media and screens has driven states and districts toward 'bell-to-bell' phone bans and is now extending to scrutiny of ed tech and screen-based education generally.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The anti-screen movement is broadening from phones to classroom technology spending.
insights.quote: the move to limit digital technology in childhood has also led parents to scrutinize educational technology, or “ed tech,” and, ultimately, rethink screen-based education altogether
insights.locator: Over the past decade, as new research

insights.claim: AI is arriving in U.S. schools amid steady policymaker pressure for rapid, complete curriculum integration, even though parents have not been consulted.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A demand-side mismatch between policy push and parental preference creates reversal risk for AI ed-tech.
insights.quote: there has been steady pressure by some policymakers to rapidly and completely integrate AI into the curriculum

insights.claim: Nearly 4 in 10 U.S. K-12 students attend schools where AI is allowed or required, 15% attend schools that block it, and 45% attend schools with no official AI policy.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Policy on AI is unsettled in nearly half of schools, so parental pressure can still shape outcomes.
insights.quote: The largest portion of American students, 45%, attend schools where no official action has been taken.

themes.theme: Parents want less AI, later, confined to labs

insights.claim: 56% of parents want AI fully blocked in schools, 26% want less than currently used, and only 13% want more.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Strong headwind for K-12 AI product adoption.
insights.quote: A majority (56%) of parents want AI fully blocked in schools

insights.claim: 38% of parents favor a books-and-handwriting classroom with AI confined to a computer lab, 25% want books and handwriting only, and just 11% want the tablet-plus-AI model.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Suggests a shift away from one-to-one devices toward shared labs and print.
insights.quote: Only 11% of parents want this form of education for their kids.

insights.claim: More than 2 in 3 parents want AI introduced only in high school or later, or not at all, with just 3% favoring kindergarten and 9% elementary school.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Products targeting younger grades face the weakest demand.
insights.quote: More than 2 in 3 parents want AI introduced in high school or later, or not at all.

themes.theme: Harms outweigh benefits and bipartisan pause support

insights.claim: 77% of parents say AI will undermine learning, 79% that it will enable malicious student behavior and 73% that it will expose children to serious risks, versus 46% expecting personalized learning, 39% creativity gains and 51% workforce preparation.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Parents see risk far more than value, undercutting core AI ed-tech marketing claims.
insights.quote: 77% say that AI will undermine learning, 79% say that AI will enable malicious behavior by students, and 73% say it will expose children to serious risks
insights.locator: 5. Parents think that AI is more likely

insights.claim: Pausing AI in schools, as New York City and Los Angeles did, is supported by 75% of Republican and 72% of Democratic parents, so it is not a partisan policy despite originating in 'deep blue' cities.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: AI moratoria could spread to red and blue districts alike.
insights.quote: 75% of Republican parents support the policy to pause AI in schools, as do 72% of Democratic parents

insights.claim: 6 in 10 parents of school-age children say AI in education makes their child's future look 'bleak' (35%) or 'frightening' (25%), citing technology doing the thinking and AI taking the most important jobs.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Widespread family-level AI pessimism is a political and consumer-sentiment risk for AI firms.
insights.quote: for 6 in 10 parents with school-age children, AI fosters a negative view of their child’s future
insights.locator: 7. AI in education gives most parents
